vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits in the leather chair with his hands folded in his lap, a habit he's developed over the past three years-something to do with his hands so they don't shake. At sixty-five, he has the weathered look of someone who's spent decades managing timelines and people, but his eyes carry a particular kind of exhaustion that has nothing to do with work.

His daughter Sophie was eight years old when the meningitis diagnosis came. Marcus remembers the hospital call with perfect clarity-he was in a project meeting when his wife rang, her voice fractured in a way he'd never heard before. He left immediately, abandoning his laptop mid-presentation, something he'd never done in forty years of work. Within hours, Sophie was in the pediatric ICU, her small body connected to machines that beeped with an urgency that matched his racing heart.

Those three weeks in the hospital exist in Marcus's mind as a kind of suspended reality. He and his wife took shifts sleeping in the uncomfortable chair beside Sophie's bed. He remembers the texture of the hospital blanket, the particular hum of the ventilator, the smell of antiseptic that he still catches sometimes in unexpected places-a cleaning supply aisle, a doctor's office-and his chest tightens immediately. Sophie recovered. She's twenty-six now, healthy, living in another city. By any measure, they were fortunate. But Marcus couldn't seem to move past it.

His wife, Elena, died five years ago from a stroke. He found her on the kitchen floor on a Tuesday morning. That loss, while devastating, felt different to him-it was the natural order of things, the way life sometimes goes. But Sophie's illness had shattered something fundamental in how he understood safety and control. For decades, Marcus had managed projects by breaking them into manageable pieces, identifying risks, creating contingencies. But you cannot manage a child's life-threatening illness. You cannot control meningitis with a spreadsheet.

In the years since Sophie's hospital stay, Marcus has developed a pattern he doesn't quite recognize as problematic until someone mentions it. He checks news reports obsessively-not just current events, but medical stories, disease outbreaks, anything that might threaten his children or grandchildren. He's become hypervigilant about health, noticing every cough or complaint from people around him. When his son mentioned a headache last month, Marcus's mind immediately went to meningitis, and he couldn't sleep that night despite his son's reassurance that it was just tension.

At work, his colleagues have noticed changes. He's become more rigid in his management style, insisting on excessive documentation and contingency planning even for minor projects. He's also become more withdrawn, declining after-work drinks and social events. The irony isn't lost on him-he's trying to manage unpredictability through control, even though he learned in the most painful way possible that this doesn't work.

Marcus avoids hospitals now, even for routine appointments. He's missed some medical checkups he probably shouldn't have. When his doctor mentioned a routine screening, he found reasons to reschedule. The thought of being in that environment-the sounds, the smells-makes his breathing shallow and his palms sweat.

At night, he sometimes lies awake thinking about those three weeks, replaying conversations, wondering if they'd gotten Sophie to the hospital soon enough, imagining scenarios where things went differently. His wife used to hold his hand during these episodes. Now he lies alone in the dark, his mind circling back to a moment he cannot change, to a fear he cannot quite release.
